posts.title: Clients buy outcomes, not email marketing

copy.default:
I do not think most appointment-led businesses actually want email marketing.

They want the commercial outcome underneath it.

A good enquiry should not disappear because nobody followed up properly.
A cancellation should have a sensible route back.
A satisfied client should not be forgotten simply because they did not remember to rebook.
A dormant regular should be identifiable before the relationship is completely cold.

Email can help with some of that.

So can SMS.
A better booking route can help.
Clearer ownership can help.
Better timing can help.

That is why I increasingly prefer the language Revenue Recovery.

The tool is secondary.

The real job is to find a commercially meaningful moment where existing intent or an existing relationship is being wasted, then build the simplest sensible system to reduce that loss.

posts.title: Lesson: stop rules are part of customer experience

copy.default:
Retention School: Stop rules are part of customer experience.

A lifecycle journey needs to know when its job is finished.

Customer books? Stop the recovery sequence.
Customer replies and a team member takes ownership? Pause the automation.
Customer declines? Respect the answer.
Customer opts out? Stop.
The relevant window passes? End the journey.
The customer moves into a different state? Reclassify them.

It is easy to judge automation by whether messages send on time.

But technically reliable messaging can still feel careless when the system ignores what happened next.

A useful trigger knows when to begin.

A useful stop rule knows when continuing would no longer help.

Good lifecycle design is not only about when to contact somebody.

It is also about knowing when to leave them alone.
